Too much camera movement. It makes it very difficult to watch. Your viewer's eye will fixate on various different things throughout the video and then it's farther away, or only visible from a different angle, or out of the shot altogether. Videos like this work better if you compose them in different shots. Start out by deciding what you want to show (and make these decisions before you start recording).

For example, let's say you want to show the first army with siege engines, the launching of the projectiles, the flight of the projectiles, the impact of the projectiles, the enemy army, and the progression of the devastation. You know how the armies are lined up (roughly) so then you decide which camera position is going to give you the footage you want for each of these shots. Position your camera and then leave it alone for 5 seconds minimum before relocating for the next shot. Edit out most (if not all) of the camera movement transitions and voila. Easy to watch, full of action, transitions from shot to shot in a sensible and meaningful way, and doesn't upset the viewer with too much movement. (Learning to decide how long to make each shot so as to not upset your viewer be ending the shot too soon is another skill altogether.)

Edit out the camera movement. That's why it's important to have a general plan before you start recording. Record a shot, move the camera straight to the next location, record the shot, etc. Then when you're done recording, edit out all the moves. If you know where you're moving the camera ahead of time, you won't be spending much time moving the camera and the viewer isn't going to miss out on much of the action because of what you've clipped out. The viewer isn't going to mind missing 20% of the encounter if the 80% they do see is comprised of clean, composed shots.
